explanations.answer: A spirit of distress from the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The Spirit of the LORD departs from Saul, and then "…a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him." (1 Samuel 16:14) This is a heavy moment for him. I think it's a hard place to be, and the story is only getting started.

explanations.answer: A sickness sent by his enemies
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend. Kings in stories always seem to have enemies lurking around. But the text gives no enemy here. It says "…a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him." (1 Samuel 16:14) This one is a heavy moment for Saul, so we'll just let the text say it.

Not in this verse, friend. Here the text says "…a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him." (1 Samuel 16:14) That's what follows when the Spirit of the LORD departs from Saul. No dream is mentioned, so no puzzle to solve. Just a heavy moment, and I think it's a hard one.

Yes, his servants. They say, "Surely a spirit of distress from God is tormenting you." (1 Samuel 16:15) They're the ones who step up and say it plainly. I think that took some nerve, because saying that to a king is like telling your boss his tie is crooked, only way heavier.

Samuel, the LORD's prophet, is busy anointing David just before this scene (1 Samuel 16:13). But in this passage the ones who speak up are Saul's servants. They tell him, "Surely a spirit of distress from God is tormenting you." (1 Samuel 16:15) Samuel doesn't say a word here.

Jonathan isn't in this passage at all, friend. The speakers here are Saul's servants, and they say, "Surely a spirit of distress from God is tormenting you." (1 Samuel 16:15) Jonathan, Saul's son (1 Samuel 13:16), is a name to keep in your back pocket, because we're not done with this story. For now, it's just the servants talking.

Right on, baker. They want "…someone who can skillfully play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:16) Whenever the distress is upon Saul, that person plays, and the servants say Saul will be well. A harp is a gentle fix for a heavy problem, and I'm a little jealous, since all I've got is a stamp and a mustache.

Nope, no dreams in this plan, friend. The servants ask for "…someone who can skillfully play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:16) They say that whenever the spirit of distress is upon Saul, he is to play it, and Saul will be well. It's all about the music here.

Ointments sound like a good guess, but that's not what the servants ask for. They say to seek out "…someone who can skillfully play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:16) The plan is music, plain and simple. Whenever the spirit of distress is upon Saul, the harp gets played, and the servants say he will be well.

Not quite, friend. Saul doesn't turn it down at all. The text says Saul commanded his servants, "Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me." (1 Samuel 16:17) He takes the plan and tells them to go find the player.
That's right, baker. Saul doesn't turn the plan down. He tells his servants, "Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me." (1 Samuel 16:17) He takes the advice and puts them to work.

That's the one, baker. The servant says, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:18) Jesse is the father, and Bethlehem is the town. Notice the servant doesn't name David yet. He just says "…a son of Jesse…"

Elkanah does show up in 1 Samuel. He's the father of Samuel the prophet (1 Samuel 1:19-20). But the servant here says, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:18) Different dad for this harp player, friend.

Eli was a priest at Shiloh, and he's in the early chapters of 1 Samuel (1 Samuel 1:9). But this servant says, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:18) So the harp player's father is Jesse, not Eli.

Yes, baker. The servant finishes with "…and the LORD is with him." (1 Samuel 16:18) Out of everything on that list, that's the line that matters most. It's the last thing he says, and it's the one that sticks.

Good guess, since a king is who the servant is talking to. But the servant says, "…and the LORD is with him." (1 Samuel 16:18) Saul is the king in this scene, and he's the one asking for a harp player. The last item on the list is about the LORD.

A prophet is in the neighborhood of this story, since Samuel anointed David just before (1 Samuel 16:13). But the servant says, "…and the LORD is with him." (1 Samuel 16:18) That's the last thing on his list. The servant doesn't mention a prophet at all.

explanations.answer: Bread and wine and a young goat
explanations.explanation: That's the spread, baker. "…Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat and sent them to Saul with his son David." (1 Samuel 16:20) So it's bread, wine and a young goat, all riding on one donkey. A donkey hauling a gift for the king is quite the delivery.

explanations.answer: Gold and silver and fine robes
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a king's gift, friend, but it's not what Jesse sends. The text says he took "…a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat…" (1 Samuel 16:20) Not a speck of gold in the list. It's a simple gift from a family in Bethlehem.

explanations.answer: Oil and honey and a calf
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, but not the list. Jesse took "…a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat…" (1 Samuel 16:20) So it's bread, wine and a young goat. The young goat is a kid, not a calf. Oil and honey aren't on that list.

It's true, baker. The text says, "…Saul loved him very much…" (1 Samuel 16:21) That happens right when David enters his service. I'll note that this is how things start out between them, and the story isn't over.

Actually, it's true, friend. The text says, "When David came to Saul and entered his service, Saul loved him very much…" (1 Samuel 16:21) So Saul loves David very much when David enters his service. The story's not finished, so I'm keeping my eyes on the oven.

Correct, baker. The text says, "…David became his armor-bearer." (1 Samuel 16:21) That's the other job Saul gives him. It's a long way from the sheep. My own career moves went from counter to drawer, so I'm not complaining.

A cupbearer is a real job in the Bible (Nehemiah 1:11), but it's not David's here. The text says, "…David became his armor-bearer." (1 Samuel 16:21) So he's carrying armor for the king, not cups. I'd say that's a step up from sheep.

David is good with a harp, but a scribe, the one who writes things down, isn't his extra job. The text says, "…David became his armor-bearer." (1 Samuel 16:21) He's near the king in a very different way, and I think he's about to learn a lot.

explanations.answer: To let David stay in his service
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Saul sends word to Jesse, "Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him." (1 Samuel 16:22) He's not just borrowing David for the afternoon. He wants him to stay.

explanations.answer: To send his older sons as well
explanations.explanation: Saul doesn't ask for more of Jesse's sons, friend. His message says, "Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him." (1 Samuel 16:22) It's all about David. One son made quite the impression.

explanations.answer: To come and live at the palace
explanations.explanation: Saul's message doesn't ask that, friend. It says, "Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him." (1 Samuel 16:22) The request is about David staying, and Jesse coming along isn't part of what Saul says.

Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite. "…Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would depart from him." (1 Samuel 16:23) So when David plays, things get better for Saul, not worse. The harp is doing its job.

That's right, baker. David plays, and "…Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would depart from him." (1 Samuel 16:23) So the servants' plan works. Relief for Saul, all because of David's harp.
